analysis.one_liner: Extends US criminal law to private contractors who commit serious crimes in war zones.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 389–30 on October 4, 2007, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill closes a gap in the Military Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Act, the 2000 law that lets the US prosecute civilians who commit crimes while accompanying troops abroad. The old law only covered employees supporting the Defense Department and troops; this bill extends it to employees of any federal agency's contractor — including the private security guards who worked in Iraq and Afghanistan — when they commit offenses that would carry more than a year in prison. It also orders the Justice Department's internal watchdog to report on how many complaints and cases against contractors it has handled, and directs the FBI to set up investigative teams in each war theater to look into alleged crimes and deaths involving contractor gunfire.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people affected by the war effort: families and comrades of people killed or harmed by contractor personnel, Iraqi and Afghan civilians seeking US accountability for contractor shootings, and taxpayers who pay for these contracts and want serious misconduct actually prosecuted. Honest contractors also gain a clearer, uniform rule instead of a patchwork.

how_it_helps.text: Makes contract personnel of any federal agency criminally answerable under US law, wherever the Armed Forces conduct a contingency operation, for conduct that would be a felony in the United States.
Requires the DOJ Inspector General to report to Congress on complaints received, investigations opened, cases closed, and every charge brought against contractors working in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Directs the FBI to create Theater Investigative Units in each war theater to investigate alleged criminal misconduct and fatalities from contractor use of force, and to refer cases to the Attorney General.
Requires the FBI to report annually on misconduct reports received, cases referred, and any legal changes it needs, so Congress can see whether contractor accountability is actually happening.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies that contract abroad — chiefly Defense and State — and taxpayers, who fund the FBI's new investigative units and reporting. Contractor employees themselves bear personal criminal liability for serious offenses committed in war zones.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only offenses punishable by more than one year in prison, so lower-level misconduct by contractor personnel stays outside the law even though that is where complaints often arise.
A Republican motion to recommit added a provision stating that nothing in the act affects intelligence activities that were otherwise permissible, narrowing the bill's reach before passage.

Investigating US-crimes in an active war zone is costly and hard: the FBI must staff and secure units in each theater, request Defense Department security when it cannot protect them, and coordinate with multiple agencies — expenses and practical burdens the bill acknowledges but does not fully solve.
The effective date covers contracts under way at enactment, and agencies got only 90 days to comply, a short runway for building investigative capacity in the middle of ongoing operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is simple and targeted: apply existing US criminal law to a workforce — armed contractors in war zones — that had largely operated outside it. The direct costs are modest (FBI units, Inspector General reports), and the carve-out for intelligence activities and the one-year prison threshold leave real gaps. The larger problem was not the design but the fate: a 389–30 House mandate that never got a Senate vote.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a vote of 389–30, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never voted, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 15, 2007, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which ordered it reported as amended by voice vote in August and formally reported it on September 27, 2007.

The bill amends the Military Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Act so that employees of contractors of any federal agency — not just those supporting Defense and the armed forces — are criminally liable under US law for serious offenses committed in or near areas of contingency operations.
On October 4, 2007, the House agreed to a motion to recommit with instructions 342–75, adding a rule-of-construction provision protecting otherwise permissible intelligence activities.
The House then passed the bill 389–30: all 225 voting Democrats voted yes, and 164 of 201 Republicans voted yes, with 30 Republicans opposed.
The Senate received the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, where it remained without a vote through the end of the 110th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contractor personnel and the firms employing them in Iraq and Afghanistan remained outside the criminal-law expansion, because the bill never reached a Senate vote.

industries.industry: Private security contractors in war zones
industries.note: Firms like the armed guards protecting US personnel in Iraq and Afghanistan would have had their employees made criminally answerable under US law for serious offenses, ending a stretch in which many such personnel fell outside any US criminal jurisdiction. Their interest in avoiding that liability ran directly against accountability for killings and abuses.

industries.industry: Federal contractors generally (logistics, reconstruction, services abroad)
industries.note: The bill reaches any federal-agency contractor workforce in contingency areas, but only for conduct that would be a serious felony in the United States. Law-abiding firms face little added burden, and they gain clear rules where the old law left gaps.

Agencies must cooperate with FBI investigative units and coordinate their inspector-general inquiries, adding oversight duties they did not previously face, while the public gains a record of contractor misconduct in Iraq and Afghanistan.
